binders: The proposition is universal over a natural number n.
It is universal over four functions coeff, f, deltaNum, deltaDen : Fin n -> Real, so each is an n-component real vector.
It is universal over two real numbers epsilonNum and epsilonDen.
hypotheses: For every i in Fin n, |deltaNum_i| <= epsilonNum |coeff_i f_i|.
For every i in Fin n, |deltaDen_i| <= epsilonDen |coeff_i|.
The exact numerator sum sum_i coeff_i f_i is nonzero.
The exact denominator sum sum_i coeff_i is nonzero.
conclusions: The relative error satisfies |Q_delta - Q| / |Q| <= (epsilonNum C(coeff,f) + epsilonDen C(coeff,1)) / (1 - epsilonDen C(coeff,1)).
mathematical_definitions: Let I_n = Fin n = {0,...,n-1}. Every sum below is over i in I_n.
For n-component real vectors ell and g, define S(ell,g) = sum_i ell_i g_i.
Define the exact quotient Q = S(coeff,f) / S(coeff,1) = (sum_i coeff_i f_i) / (sum_i coeff_i).
Define the perturbed quotient Q_delta = (sum_i (coeff_i f_i + deltaNum_i)) / (sum_i (coeff_i + deltaDen_i)).
All absolute values are ordinary scalar real absolute values; sum_i |ell_i g_i| is an l1-type sum of scalar magnitudes, not a separately introduced vector norm.
translation.proposition_plain_english: For every dimension n, coefficient vector coeff, value vector f, additive numerator and denominator perturbation vectors deltaNum and deltaDen, and nonnegative perturbation levels epsilonNum and epsilonDen, suppose each numerator perturbation is bounded pointwise by epsilonNum times the magnitude of coeff_i f_i and each denominator perturbation is bounded pointwise by epsilonDen times the magnitude of coeff_i. If both the exact numerator sum and exact denominator sum are nonzero and epsilonDen times the denominator amplification factor C(coeff,1) is strictly less than one, then the relative absolute error between the perturbed quotient Q_delta and exact quotient Q is at most (epsilonNum C(coeff,f) + epsilonDen C(coeff,1)) divided by (1 - epsilonDen C(coeff,1)).

restrictions_and_vacuity_risks: Although n may syntactically be zero, for n = 0 both finite sums are zero, so the two nonzero hypotheses cannot hold and the implication is vacuous.

The proposition applies only when both sum_i coeff_i f_i and sum_i coeff_i are nonzero. Consequently Q, C(coeff,f), C(coeff,1), and the relative-error denominator |Q| have nonzero mathematical denominators.
The strict condition epsilonDen C(coeff,1) < 1 makes the right-hand denominator 1 - epsilonDen C(coeff,1) positive.

No explicit nonzero hypothesis is stated for the perturbed denominator sum_i (coeff_i + deltaDen_i); the denominator perturbation bound together with the strict smallness condition implies that it cannot vanish.
The perturbation assumptions are componentwise relative bounds. In particular, coeff_i f_i = 0 forces deltaNum_i = 0, and coeff_i = 0 forces deltaDen_i = 0.
No sign restrictions are imposed on coefficients, values, or perturbations.

The assertion concerns exact real arithmetic with prescribed additive perturbations. It does not encode a floating-point format, rounding mode, evaluation order, probabilistic model, or a claim that the bound is sharp.
The theorem is an implication and says nothing for inputs failing any hypothesis.
There are no existential quantifiers or witness choices in the proposition.
